claim: RNA associated with mitotic chromosomes is concentrated at pericentric heterochromatin in HeLa cells.
source: The EU-RNA signal we detected on human mitotic chromosomes, although distributed in distinct puncta along chromosome arms, was particularly concentrated around centromeres (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing EU-RNA labeling concentrated at centromeric regions in microscopy images (Figure 1A).

claim: Chromosome-associated RNA in mitotic cells is sensitive to RNase A treatment.
source: The RNA signal was sensitive to treatment with Ribonuclease (RNase) A, confirming that our EU treatment specifically labeled RNA; but not sensitive to RNase III or RNase H, indicating that this RNA possesses single-stranded (ssRNA) regions but not nuclease-accessible double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) or RNA-DNA hybrids (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing loss of signal after RNase A treatment but not after RNase III or RNase H treatment.

claim: Four out of eight different cell lines showed RNA enrichment at pericentric regions.
source: Four out of eight different cell lines showed RNA enrichment at pericentric regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from testing multiple cell lines.

claim: Both primary fibroblasts and HeLa cells exhibited pericentric RNA localization.
source: Both primary fibroblasts and HeLa cells exhibited pericentric RNA localization, indicating that this phenomenon is not specific to immortalized cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from both primary and immortalized cell lines.

claim: α-satellite RNA is detected at pericentric heterochromatin on human mitotic chromosomes.
source: We detected RNA FISH signal with two different α-satellite probes, one of which was specific for the pericentric α-satellite array D1Z5 (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) (Pironon et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by RNA FISH experimental data showing α-satellite RNA signal at pericentric regions.

claim: α-satellite RNA FISH signal is sensitive to RNase treatment.
source: This signal was sensitive to RNase treatment (Figure 1D) and colocalized with H3K9me3 staining (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), but not with HEC1 staining that labels the core centromere/kinetochore (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing loss of RNA FISH signal after RNase treatment.

claim: α-satellite RNA colocalizes with H3K9me3 but not with HEC1.
source: This signal was sensitive to RNase treatment (Figure 1D) and colocalized with H3K9me3 staining (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), but not with HEC1 staining that labels the core centromere/kinetochore (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing overlap with H3K9me3 but not HEC1.

claim: α-satellite RNA is localized in cis at the site of its transcription.
source: We also observed that α-satellite RNA was localized in cis (i.e. at the same site of its transcription), as we saw that the RNA FISH signal was constrained to only the chromosomes known to contain the specific α-satellite DNA sequences recognized by our probes (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by RNA FISH data showing signal only on chromosomes containing the corresponding α-satellite DNA sequences.

claim: Most of the pericentric RNA signal is transcribed by RNA polymerase I.
source: We measured a reduction of approximately 50% in pericentric RNA signal after treatment with α-amanitin or triptolide – which preferentially inhibit Pol II – but observed a complete loss of signal after treatment with actinomycin D or CX-5461 – which preferentially inhibit Pol I, and show no detectable Pol II inhibition (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B). Thus, most of the pericentric RNA signal we observe appears to be transcribed by Pol I.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential effects of RNA polymerase inhibitors on pericentric RNA signal.

claim: Pericentric RNA is transcribed within 4 hours before mitosis.
source: We found that continuous EU labeling for 8 or 4 hr before mitosis led to pericentric EU-RNA signal, but a 4 hr EU pulse followed by a 4 hr chase resulted in no EU-RNA signal on mitotic chromosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D). This suggests that the pericentric RNA we observe on mitotic chromosomes is transcribed within the 4 hr before mitosis, or that it is transcribed earlier but dissociates from chromosomes in the 4 hr washout period after labeling.
evidence: Supported by pulse-chase experimental data showing timing of RNA synthesis.

claim: RNase A treatment reduces the pericentric localization of SUV39H1 to 43% of untreated control.
source: We found that RNase A treatment reduced the pericentric localization of SUV39H1 to 43 ± 4% of the untreated control, and that SUV39H1 localization could be completely rescued by adding specific RNase inhibitors (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative microscopy data measuring SUV39H1 localization after RNase treatment.

claim: SUV39H1 localization can be completely rescued by adding RNase inhibitors after RNase A treatment.
source: We found that RNase A treatment reduced the pericentric localization of SUV39H1 to 43 ± 4% of the untreated control, and that SUV39H1 localization could be completely rescued by adding specific RNase inhibitors (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing restoration of SUV39H1 localization with RNase inhibitors.

claim: DNA staining at pericentric regions is not reduced by RNase A treatment.
source: DNA staining at pericentric regions was not reduced in this experiment, indicating that the general chromosome structure at pericentric heterochromatin was not disrupted by RNase A treatment (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative microscopy data showing no change in DNA signal after RNase treatment.

claim: Total SUV39H1 protein levels are not affected by RNase A treatment.
source: We also determined that total SUV39H1 protein levels are not affected by RNase A treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1M).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing no change in SUV39H1 protein levels.

claim: SUV39H1 depends on the presence of RNA for its localization on human mitotic chromosomes.
source: These data demonstrate that SUV39H1 depends on the presence of RNA for its localization on human mitotic chromosomes.
evidence: Inferred from RNase treatment experiments showing reduced SUV39H1 localization.

claim: H3K9me3 levels are substantially reduced in human SUV39 DKO cells.
source: As observed in SUV39 double null mouse cells (Lachner et al., 2001; Peters et al., 2001), both H3K9me3 levels and HP1α localization were substantially reduced in human SUV39 DKO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, D, E, H and K).
evidence: Supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data from SUV39 DKO cells, and cited previous findings in mouse cells.

claim: HP1α localization is substantially reduced in human SUV39 DKO cells.
source: As observed in SUV39 double null mouse cells (Lachner et al., 2001; Peters et al., 2001), both H3K9me3 levels and HP1α localization were substantially reduced in human SUV39 DKO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, D, E, H and K).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data from SUV39 DKO cells, and cited previous findings in mouse cells.

claim: Levels of centromeric satellite RNA, including α-satellite RNA, increased in SUV39 DKO cells.
source: However, the levels of centromeric satellite RNA, including α-satellite RNA, increased in SUV39 DKO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, F and J) (Lee et al., 1997), consistent with SUV39H1/SUV39H2 loss causing defective heterochromatin and transcriptional depression of centromeric satellites.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and RNA-seq data from SUV39 DKO cells, and cited previous findings.

claim: No significant changes in global RNA expression levels were observed in SUV39 DKO cells.
source: In contrast to the de-repression of satellite RNA, we saw no significant changes in global RNA expression levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data comparing SUV39 DKO and control cells.

claim: α-satellite RNA continues to localize to pericentric heterochromatin in the absence of SUV39H1 and SUV39H2.
source: In the absence of SUV39H1 and SUV39H2, α-satellite RNA continued to localize to pericentric heterochromatin as assayed by RNA FISH (Figure 2—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: Supported by RNA FISH data from SUV39 DKO cells.

claim: The chromodomain of SUV39H1 is sufficient for RNA binding activity.
source: From these data, we conclude that the chromodomain, SUV39H1 42–106, is sufficient for RNA binding activity.
evidence: Inferred from EMSA data showing RNA binding by the chromodomain fragment.

claim: SUV39H1 truncations containing the chromodomain bound to RNA with the highest affinity.
source: We found that the SUV39H1 truncations containing the chromodomain bound to RNA with the highest affinity, whereas the C-terminal fragment showed no detectable binding (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data comparing different SUV39H1 truncations.

claim: The N-terminal extension plus chromodomain of SUV39H1 (1-106) has a dissociation constant of 0.15 ± 0.01 µM for RNA.
source: The addition of the N-terminal extension to the chromodomain of SUV39H1 (1–106) provided a 16-fold increase in affinity relative to the chromodomain alone (42-106), with dissociation constants (Kd) of 0.15 ± 0.01 µM and 2.31 ± 0.17 µM, respectively.
evidence: Supported by quantitative EMSA data measuring binding affinity.

claim: The chromodomain alone of SUV39H1 (42-106) has a dissociation constant of 2.31 ± 0.17 µM for RNA.
source: The addition of the N-terminal extension to the chromodomain of SUV39H1 (1–106) provided a 16-fold increase in affinity relative to the chromodomain alone (42-106), with dissociation constants (Kd) of 0.15 ± 0.01 µM and 2.31 ± 0.17 µM, respectively.
evidence: Supported by quantitative EMSA data measuring binding affinity.

claim: SUV39H1 1-106 binds to all five types of nucleic acids (ssRNA, ssDNA, dsRNA, dsDNA, RNA/DNA hybrids) with similar affinities.
source: We found that SUV39H1 1–106 bound to all five types of nucleic acids with similar affinities, ranging from 61 ± 5 nM for ssRNA to 185 ± 17 nM for dsDNA (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data testing different nucleic acid types.

claim: SUV39H1 1-106 bound α-satellite RNA with a dissociation constant of 23 ± 2 nM.
source: We found that SUV39H1 1–106 bound α-satellite or β-actin RNA with similar affinities: 23 ± 2 nM and 32 ± 2 nM, respectively (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data measuring binding to α-satellite RNA.

claim: SUV39H1 1-106 bound β-actin RNA with a dissociation constant of 32 ± 2 nM.
source: We found that SUV39H1 1–106 bound α-satellite or β-actin RNA with similar affinities: 23 ± 2 nM and 32 ± 2 nM, respectively (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data measuring binding to β-actin RNA.

claim: SUV39H1 can bind both double- and single-stranded nucleic acids with minimal sequence preference.
source: We conclude that SUV39H1 can bind both double- and single-stranded nucleic acids, has minimal sequence preference for the sequences tested thus far, and that binding affinity increases with increasing nucleic acid length (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Inferred from EMSA data showing similar binding to different sequences and nucleic acid types.

claim: SUV39H1 binding affinity increases with increasing nucleic acid length.
source: We conclude that SUV39H1 can bind both double- and single-stranded nucleic acids, has minimal sequence preference for the sequences tested thus far, and that binding affinity increases with increasing nucleic acid length (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by EMSA data comparing binding to 19mer, 50mer, and 180mer nucleic acids.

claim: The R55A and R84A mutations almost completely abolished RNA binding by SUV39H1.
source: By performing a more comprehensive analysis of the binding of these 23 mutants (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), we discovered two mutations, R55A and R84A, that almost completely abolished RNA binding by SUV39H1, reducing the affinity over 40-fold compared to WT (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by EMSA and filter binding assay data comparing mutant and WT SUV39H1.

claim: Neither SUV39H1R55A nor SUV39H1R84A alter the binding of SUV39H1 to H3K9me3.
source: Importantly, neither of the nucleic acid binding mutants (SUV39H1R55A and SUV39H1R84A) alter the binding of SUV39H1 to H3K9me3 (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Supported by peptide binding assay data showing no change in H3K9me3 binding for these mutants.

claim: The aromatic cage mutant SUV39H1F43A completely disrupts binding to H3K9me3.
source: As previously reported, we found that the WT SUV39H1 chromodomain preferentially binds to H3K9me3 compared to H3K9me0, and this binding is completely disrupted by the aromatic cage mutant SUV39H1F43A (Figure 4E and F) (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by peptide binding assay data and cited previous findings.

claim: The R55A, R84A, and F43A mutations had no effect on the methyltransferase activity of full-length SUV39H1.
source: We also confirmed that the R55A, R84A, and F43A mutations had no effect on the methyltransferase activity of full-length SUV39H1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by histone methyltransferase assay data.

claim: The addition of RNA inhibits SUV39H1 methyltransferase activity.
source: Interestingly, the addition of RNA inhibits SUV39H1 activity, as has been previously shown for PRC2 and several other SET domain histone methyltransferases (Cifuentes-Rojas et al., 2014; Kaneko et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by histone methyltransferase assay data and cited previous findings.

claim: SUV39H1 colocalizes with EU-labeled RNA at pericentric regions of mitotic chromosomes.
source: In SUV39H1-GFP expressing HeLa cells, SUV39H1 colocalizes with EU-labeled RNA at pericentric regions of mitotic chromosomes (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data showing colocalization.

claim: α-satellite RNA was enriched 13 ± 2 fold in the WT SUV39H1 IP compared to GFP alone.
source: We found that α-satellite RNA was enriched in the WT SUV39H1 IP 13 ± 2 fold when compared to GFP alone (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and that R55A mutation reduced the amount of α-satellite RNA to 45 ± 16% of the levels bound to WT (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by RNA immunoprecipitation and RT-qPCR data.

claim: The R55A mutation reduced the amount of α-satellite RNA bound to SUV39H1 to 45 ± 16% of WT levels.
source: We found that α-satellite RNA was enriched in the WT SUV39H1 IP 13 ± 2 fold when compared to GFP alone (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and that R55A mutation reduced the amount of α-satellite RNA to 45 ± 16% of the levels bound to WT (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by RNA immunoprecipitation and RT-qPCR data.

claim: The R55A mutation did not disrupt SUV39H1's association with HP1α.
source: In addition, the R55A mutation did not disrupt SUV39H1's association with HP1α, indicating that α-satellite RNA binding to SUV39H1 is not occurring indirectly through HP1α (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing HP1α binding to SUV39H1R55A.

claim: SUV39H1 associates with α-satellite RNA in cells.
source: These results demonstrate that SUV39H1 associates with α-satellite RNA in cells, and that this association is facilitated by the nucleic acid binding activity of the SUV39H1 chromodomain.
evidence: Inferred from RNA immunoprecipitation data showing enrichment of α-satellite RNA with SUV39H1.

claim: The R55A and R84A nucleic acid binding mutants of SUV39H1 showed defects in localization, reducing SUV39H1 signal to about half of WT levels.
source: The R55A and R84A nucleic acid binding mutants of SUV39H1 showed defects in localization, reducing SUV39H1 signal by about half (R55A: 42 ± 8% of WT levels, R84A: 45 ± 9% of WT levels) (Figure 6A, B and C); indicating that the direct interaction of SUV39H1 with nucleic acids is important for its localization to pericentric heterochromatin.
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence microscopy data.

claim: The aromatic cage mutants W64A and F43A led to more pronounced localization defects than the nucleic acid binding mutants.
source: We also found that the aromatic cage mutants W64A and F43A led to more pronounced localization defects than those caused by the nucleic acid binding mutants (W64A: 10 ± 4% of WT levels, F43A: 15 ± 5% of WT levels) (Figure 6A, B and C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence microscopy data.

claim: Both H3K9me3 binding and nucleic acid binding contribute to SUV39H1 localization to pericentric heterochromatin during mitosis.
source: These results suggest that both H3K9me3 binding and nucleic acid binding contribute to SUV39H1 localization to pericentric heterochromatin during mitosis.
evidence: Inferred from localization data comparing different SUV39H1 mutants.

claim: RNase A treatment reduced the pericentric localization of WT SUV39H1 to 43 ± 4% of the undigested control.
source: RNase A treatment reduced the pericentric localization of SUV39H1 to 43 ± 4% of the undigested control, similar to the levels of the untreated SUV39H1R55A mutant in the same experiments (52 ± 9% of WT) (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence microscopy data.

claim: RNase A treatment did not significantly reduce the amount of SUV39H1R55A at pericentric chromatin.
source: This is further supported by the fact that RNase A treatment did not significantly reduce the amount of SUV39H1R55A at pericentric chromatin (untreated: 52 ± 9%, RNase A: 42 ± 5%) (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence microscopy data.

claim: Direct binding to both chromosome-associated RNA and H3K9me2/3 are required for proper localization of SUV39H1 to pericentric heterochromatin.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that direct binding to both chromosome-associated RNA and H3K9me2/3 are required for proper localization of SUV39H1 to pericentric heterochromatin.
evidence: Inferred from combined data on RNase treatment and mutant localization.

claim: HP1α localization at heterochromatin is sensitive to RNase treatment.
source: Previous studies found that HP1α localization at heterochromatin is sensitive to RNase treatment in both mouse interphase cells and on human mitotic chromosomes (Maison et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2007). We also observed a reduction in HP1α levels on chromatin after RNase A treatment, to 77 ± 13% of control levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data and cited previous findings.

claim: Expressing SUV39H1-GFP for 6 hours caused a 1.5-fold increase in HP1α localization.
source: Consistent with this, expressing SUV39H1-GFP for 6 hr, which causes an increase in SUV39H1-GFP at pericentric regions, also caused a 1.5-fold increase in HP1α localization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B), in the absence of any detectable change in H3K9me3 levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data.

claim: RNase A treatment abolished the increase in HP1α localization following exogenous SUV39H1-GFP expression.
source: Additionally, we observed that RNase A treatment abolished the increase in HP1α localization following exogenous SUV39H1-GFP expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data.

claim: The extent of HP1α localization positively correlated with SUV39H1 localization after expressing SUV39H1 mutants.
source: Finally, after expressing SUV39H1 mutants, the extent of HP1α localization positively correlated with SUV39H1 localization (Figure 6A and C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data comparing different mutants.

claim: WT SUV39H1 recovered with an average half-time of 27 ± 7 s in FRAP experiments.
source: After photobleaching, WT SUV39H1 recovered with an average half-time of 27 ± 7 s (Figure 7D), with a stable, immobile fraction of SUV39H1 that did not recover during the time frame of our experiment (Figure 7B, C and E).
evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data.

claim: The mobile fraction of WT SUV39H1 represented 58 ± 7% of the total nuclear SUV39H1.
source: The mobile fraction represented 58 ± 7% of the total nuclear SUV39H1 (Figure 7E), consistent with previous measurements (Hahn et al., 2013; Krouwels et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data and cited previous findings.

claim: The aromatic cage mutant SUV39H1W64A had a recovery half-time of 6 ± 2 s.
source: The aromatic cage mutants SUV39H1W64A (Figure 7B) and SUV39H1F43A (Figure 7C), which disrupt binding to H3K9me3, had a much faster recovery half-time of 6 ± 2 and 5 ± 1 s, respectively (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data.

claim: The aromatic cage mutant SUV39H1F43A had a recovery half-time of 5 ± 1 s.
source: The aromatic cage mutants SUV39H1W64A (Figure 7B) and SUV39H1F43A (Figure 7C), which disrupt binding to H3K9me3, had a much faster recovery half-time of 6 ± 2 and 5 ± 1 s, respectively (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data.

claim: Approximately 90-95% of each aromatic cage mutant (W64A and F43A) was determined to be mobile within the nucleus.
source: Unlike WT SUV39H1, approximately 90–95% of each aromatic cage mutant was determined to be mobile within the nucleus (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data.

claim: The nucleic acid binding deficient mutant SUV39H1R55A showed an average recovery time of 14 ± 3 s.
source: Interestingly, the nucleic acid binding deficient mutants SUV39H1R55A (Figure 7B) and SUV39H1R84A (Figure 7C) showed an average recovery time in between that of WT SUV39H1 and the H3K9me3 binding mutants, with half-lives of 14 ± 3 and 13 ± 2 s, respectively (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data.

claim: The nucleic acid binding deficient mutant SUV39H1R84A showed an average recovery time of 13 ± 2 s.
source: Interestingly, the nucleic acid binding deficient mutants SUV39H1R55A (Figure 7B) and SUV39H1R84A (Figure 7C) showed an average recovery time in between that of WT SUV39H1 and the H3K9me3 binding mutants, with half-lives of 14 ± 3 and 13 ± 2 s, respectively (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data.

claim: Both SUV39H1R55A and SUV39H1R84A demonstrated a level of mobility (77% ± 6) that was greater than WT SUV39H1, but less than the aromatic cage mutants.
source: Consistent with this trend, both SUV39H1R55A and SUV39H1R84A demonstrated a level of mobility (77% ± 6) that was greater than WT SUV39H1, but less than the aromatic cage mutants SUV39H1W64A and SUV39H1F43A (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data.

claim: Direct binding to nucleic acids stabilizes the association of SUV39H1 with chromatin in interphase cells.
source: Combined with our in vitro biochemical analysis, these observations support a model in which direct binding to nucleic acids stabilizes the association of SUV39H1 with chromatin in interphase cells as well as in mitosis.
evidence: Inferred from FRAP data showing intermediate recovery kinetics for nucleic acid binding mutants.

claim: The RNA Pol I inhibitor CX-5461 decreased the fluorescence recovery half-time of WT SUV39H1 from 27 ± 7 s to 16 ± 3 s.
source: When we added the RNA Pol I inhibitor CX-5461 – a treatment that we saw reduces RNA localization on mitotic chromosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B) – the fluorescence recovery half-time of WT SUV39H1 decreased from 27 ± 7 s to 16 ± 3 s, comparable to the half-time of the nucleic acid binding mutant SUV39H1R55A (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data with RNA polymerase inhibitor treatment.

claim: Total H3K9me3 levels were reduced in all SUV39H1 mutants (R55A, F43A, R55A/F43A) compared to WT SUV39H1.
source: We found that total H3K9me3 levels, as well as H3K9me3 localization at centromeres, were reduced in all SUV39H1 mutants compared to WT SUV39H1 (Figure 8B, C, D and E), demonstrating a role for both H3K9me3 binding and nucleic acid binding by SUV39H1 in maintaining normal H3K9 methylation levels.
evidence: Supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data from endogenous SUV39H1 mutant cell lines.

claim: H3K9me3 localization at centromeres was reduced in all SUV39H1 mutants (R55A, F43A, R55A/F43A) compared to WT SUV39H1.
source: We found that total H3K9me3 levels, as well as H3K9me3 localization at centromeres, were reduced in all SUV39H1 mutants compared to WT SUV39H1 (Figure 8B, C, D and E), demonstrating a role for both H3K9me3 binding and nucleic acid binding by SUV39H1 in maintaining normal H3K9 methylation levels.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data from endogenous SUV39H1 mutant cell lines.

claim: α-satellite expression increased 1.35-fold in the R55A mutant cell line compared to WT.
source: We found that α-satellite expression increased 1.35-fold, 1.56-fold, and 2.10-fold, in the R55A, F43A, and the R55A/F43A double mutant cells lines, respectively, compared to WT (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from endogenous SUV39H1 mutant cell lines.

claim: α-satellite expression increased 1.56-fold in the F43A mutant cell line compared to WT.
source: We found that α-satellite expression increased 1.35-fold, 1.56-fold, and 2.10-fold, in the R55A, F43A, and the R55A/F43A double mutant cells lines, respectively, compared to WT (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from endogenous SUV39H1 mutant cell lines.

claim: α-satellite expression increased 2.10-fold in the R55A/F43A double mutant cell line compared to WT.
source: We found that α-satellite expression increased 1.35-fold, 1.56-fold, and 2.10-fold, in the R55A, F43A, and the R55A/F43A double mutant cells lines, respectively, compared to WT (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from endogenous SUV39H1 mutant cell lines.

claim: A significant increase in α-satellite RNA levels was observed in R55A/F43A compared to F43A.
source: Interestingly, although no change in H3K9me3 was detected between the F43A single mutant and the R55A/F43A double mutant (Figure 8C and D), a significant increase in α-satellite RNA levels was observed in R55A/F43A compared to F43A (Figure 8F), indicating that SUV39H1 nucleic binding may make H3K9me3-independent contributions to heterochromatin function.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data comparing F43A and R55A/F43A mutants.

claim: SUV39H1 nucleic acid binding may make H3K9me3-independent contributions to heterochromatin function.
source: Interestingly, although no change in H3K9me3 was detected between the F43A single mutant and the R55A/F43A double mutant (Figure 8C and D), a significant increase in α-satellite RNA levels was observed in R55A/F43A compared to F43A (Figure 8F), indicating that SUV39H1 nucleic binding may make H3K9me3-independent contributions to heterochromatin function.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of α-satellite RNA levels in F43A and R55A/F43A mutants despite similar H3K9me3 levels.

claim: Both RNA binding and H3K9me3 binding by SUV39H1 contribute to silencing of constitutive heterochromatin in human cells.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that both RNA binding and H3K9me3 binding by SUV39H1 contribute to silencing of constitutive heterochromatin in human cells.
evidence: Inferred from combined data showing increased α-satellite RNA expression in both nucleic acid binding and H3K9me3 binding mutants.

claim: Chromatin-associated RNA contributes to the localization of SUV39H1 at constitutive heterochromatin in humans.
source: In this study, we establish that chromatin-associated RNA contributes to the localization of SUV39H1 at constitutive heterochromatin in humans.
evidence: Summary statement based on multiple experimental findings throughout the study.

claim: SUV39H1 binds without any observed sequence preference to both DNA and RNA in vitro.
source: We show that SUV39H1 binds without any observed sequence preference to both DNA and RNA in vitro, and that SUV39H1 binds RNA transcribed from pericentromeric repeats in human cells.
evidence: Summary statement based on EMSA data showing similar binding to different sequences.

claim: Mutations that disrupt the nucleic acid binding function of SUV39H1 cause defects in its localization to pericentric heterochromatin.
source: Mutations that disrupt the nucleic acid binding function of SUV39H1 cause defects in its localization to pericentric heterochromatin, destabilize SUV39H1's association with chromatin, and result in heterochromatin silencing defects.
evidence: Summary statement based on localization, FRAP, and silencing data from nucleic acid binding mutants.

claim: The direct binding of SUV39H1 to RNA and to methylated histones ensures proper constitutive heterochromatin function in humans.
source: We propose a model in which the direct binding of SUV39H1 to RNA and to methylated histones ensures proper constitutive heterochromatin function in humans.
evidence: Proposed model based on combined experimental findings.

claim: SUV39 proteins catalyze the di- and tri-methylation of lysine 9 of histone H3 (H3K9me2/3).
source: SUV39 proteins catalyze the di- and tri-methylation of lysine 9 of histone H3 (H3K9me2/3), and these histone modifications are bound by chromodomain-containing proteins, including the SUV39 enzymes themselves and the HP1 family of proteins (Al-Sady et al., 2013; Bannister et al., 2001; Lachner et al., 2001; Müller et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: H3K9me2/3 modifications are bound by chromodomain-containing proteins, including SUV39 enzymes and HP1 family proteins.
source: SUV39 proteins catalyze the di- and tri-methylation of lysine 9 of histone H3 (H3K9me2/3), and these histone modifications are bound by chromodomain-containing proteins, including the SUV39 enzymes themselves and the HP1 family of proteins (Al-Sady et al., 2013; Bannister et al., 2001; Lachner et al., 2001; Müller et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: HP1 protein binding to H3K9me2/3 chromatin drives chromatin compaction and transcriptional repression through oligomerization.
source: HP1 protein binding to H3K9me2/3 chromatin is then thought to drive chromatin compaction and transcriptional repression through oligomerization (Canzio et al., 2011; Fan et al., 2004; Grewal and Jia, 2007).
evidence: Established model supported by citations.

claim: SUV39H1 and H3K9me3 are predominately associated with constitutive heterochromatin.
source: SUV39H1 and H3K9me3 are predominately associated with constitutive heterochromatin, which represses 'selfish' genetic elements and repetitive DNA to promote genomic stability (Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2014; Peters et al., 2001).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In fission yeast, disruption of pericentric heterochromatin causes chromosome cohesion defects and chromosome missegregation.
source: In fission yeast, disruption of pericentric heterochromatin causes chromosome cohesion defects and chromosome missegregation (Bernard et al., 2001); and in mammals, defective pericentric heterochromatin and aberrant transcription of pericentric repeats are associated with genomic instability and cancer (Peters et al., 2001; Ting et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In mammals, defective pericentric heterochromatin and aberrant transcription of pericentric repeats are associated with genomic instability and cancer.
source: In fission yeast, disruption of pericentric heterochromatin causes chromosome cohesion defects and chromosome missegregation (Bernard et al., 2001); and in mammals, defective pericentric heterochromatin and aberrant transcription of pericentric repeats are associated with genomic instability and cancer (Peters et al., 2001; Ting et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SUV39H1 and SUV39H2 double knockout mice exhibit reduced embryonic viability, small stature, chromosome instability, increased risk of tumor formation, and male infertility.
source: These defects in constitutive heterochromatin are most evident in SUV39H1 and SUV39H2 double knockout mice, which exhibit reduced embryonic viability, small stature, chromosome instability, an increased risk of tumor formation, and male infertility owing to defective spermatogenesis (Peters et al., 2001).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In fission yeast, the localization of pericentric heterochromatin proteins, including Clr4, relies on the RNAi machinery.
source: In fission yeast, the localization of pericentric heterochromatin proteins, including the SUV39 homolog Clr4, relies on the RNAi machinery (Bühler and Moazed, 2007; Grewal and Jia, 2007; Moazed, 2011), and RNAi has also been implicated in heterochromatin formation in other eukaryotic systems as well (Fukagawa et al., 2004; Pal-Bhadra et al., 2004).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RNA is involved in targeting SUV39H1 to telomeres and to the Oct4 locus.
source: Recent studies reported that RNA is involved in targeting SUV39H1 to telomeres and to the Oct4 locus (Porro et al., 2014; Scarola et al., 2015); however, it is unclear whether RNA plays a broader role in SUV39H1-dependent heterochromatin formation, and if direct RNA binding regulates the association of SUV39H1 with pericentric heterochromatin.
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Chromodomain-containing proteins can act as RNA binding domains.
source: This is consistent with previous findings that chromodomains can act as RNA binding domains (Akhtar et al., 2000), and that the telomeric TERRA RNA associates with SUV39H1 (Porro et al., 2014).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The chromodomains of HP1 proteins specifically recognize methylated H3K9 through three conserved aromatic residues called the 'aromatic cage'.
source: The chromodomains of HP1 proteins specifically recognize methylated H3K9 through three conserved aromatic residues, called the 'aromatic cage' (Bannister et al., 2001; Jacobs and Khorasanizadeh, 2002; Lachner et al., 2001; Nielsen et al., 2002).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The SUV39H1 chromodomain specifically binds to methylated H3K9 peptides via three aromatic cage residues.
source: The SUV39H1 chromodomain also specifically binds to methylated H3K9 peptides, most likely via three similar aromatic cage residues (Figure 4B) (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation and structural data.

claim: Transcription is largely repressed in mitosis.
source: Because transcription is largely repressed in mitosis (Gottesfeld and Forbes, 1997), RNAs bound to mitotic chromosomes may be more likely to play regulatory roles than RNAs associated with chromatin during interphase.
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Transcription by RNA polymerase II can occur from the core centromere regions of human mitotic chromosomes.
source: A previous study demonstrated that transcription by RNA polymerase II (Pol II) can occur from the core centromere regions of human mitotic chromosomes (Chan et al., 2012).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Direct RNA binding by PRC2 and HP1α is important for their proper localization and function.
source: The finding that RNA is bound to the pericentric regions of human mitotic chromosomes is intriguing in light of previous observations that direct RNA binding by the heterochromatin factors Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) and HP1α is important for their proper localization and function (Muchardt et al., 2002; Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mouse HP1α protein can directly bind RNA.
source: SUV39H1 binds directly to HP1 proteins (Yamamoto and Sonoda, 2003), and mouse HP1α protein can directly bind RNA (Muchardt et al., 2002).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The RNA-dependent mechanism for SUV39 function appears to be present in both human and mouse cells.
source: Importantly, the RNA-dependent mechanism for SUV39 function appears to be present in both human and mouse cells (Shirai et al., 2017; Velazquez Camacho et al., 2017) suggesting a conserved role for RNA in regulating constitutive heterochromatin.
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies.
